cells.tense: The connection runs both ways right now, and you're letting it stay that way.
cells.ask: Name one ending you can see coming and tell one person what it's costing you, without asking them to fix it.
cells.core:
You can feel what someone else is going through and still know where you stop and they begin. That's rarer than it sounds. Most people either go numb to stay separate or lose the line entirely. You're doing neither.

The endings around you aren't swallowing you. Something has finished or is finishing, and you're staying close to the people it touches without going under with them. That's the hard part. When it's going well, you tell someone how much they matter and still sleep in your own bed.

Keeping this costs something. The pull is to merge, to take their ending as yours, and you keep choosing contact instead. What this balance is free to feed next is holding on — staying present through the clearing without forcing the ending or rushing the renewal. Endure it with them rather than for them, and the connection stays clean.
cells.sheetLine: Connection that honors difference, not fusion.
cells.verb: feeling with others rather than only about them
cells.place: at the threshold where what's over has to be let end

cells.tense: You'll feel what their ending costs them before you've let yours land.
cells.ask: Pick one ending you're managing on someone else's behalf and let it be theirs for a week.
cells.core:
You're carrying other people's endings before they arrive. Before they've felt it, before it's even here, you've already lived through it for them, bracing for the loss on their behalf. The feeling is real. The timing is yours, not theirs.

Somewhere in there your own ending got put on hold while you cleared the way for theirs. You can't tell any more which ache started in you and which you picked up in the next room. That's not a failure of care. It's care with no wall left to stop at.

What's needed isn't to stop feeling. It's to let one thing finish without you holding it, to honor an ending instead of pre-living it. When it's going well, you can feel with someone through a loss and still be in your own life, letting what ends actually end. Hand this one back.

cells.tense: The door you're standing at was left behind a while back.
cells.ask: Tell one person one true thing about how you're actually doing, and leave the next sentence for them.
cells.core:
You can be in a room and stay at the edge of it. The exchanges are fine — warm enough, in time — but they don't land anywhere. You're not cold to people. The feeling just doesn't arrive, and after a while you stop expecting it.

There's an ending you went through and came out the other side without ever really being in it. That's when the moving stopped. You kept getting almost close and pulling back to the rim, and it's become the way you sit in the room now.

What's absent isn't a stronger feeling. It's a small adjustment, over and over — one honest word, one breath where you stay instead of leaving. When it's going well, someone's experience can meet yours and both stay whole. That comes back in small pieces, not in one doorway.

cells.tense: Others feel your care in the room while you feel nothing at all.
cells.ask: Say out loud one thing you notice about what someone close to you needs.
cells.core:
People leave conversations with you feeling seen. You'd call that just how you are — practical, not sentimental — but the care is landing in them whether or not it registers in you. You've stopped counting it as yours.

What's running underneath is a pattern you can see more clearly than most: how endings work, what has to come apart for anything to start. You read that in situations fast, almost before the people in them do. That reading is itself a way of being close.

Somewhere along the line you handed the tenderness off to the room and kept the mechanics. When it's going well, what people feel from you and what you feel are the same thing, and you don't have to perform warmth you don't yet feel. Start by admitting you see what you see.

attempts.check: What the record doesn't support: it gives me the shape of each status, not the person I'm writing for — I have no window into whose door is behind them or who they're fused with. A reader could reasonably say I've painted a life I can't see; so the cells stay on the mechanism and let them refuse the particulars. The asks survive being wrong: each is one visible act, doable alone today, useful even if its read is miscalibrated. The line I'm keeping out of the cells is the one that would serve the writing more than the person — 'you feel others' pain as your own' as a flattering portrait rather than a condition they can test.
